newsitem.title: USA: Bhutto suggests U.S. mediate Kashmir dispute.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto suggests U.S. mediate Kashmir dispute.

text.p: Pakistani Premier Benazir Bhutto urged the United States on Saturday to mediate between her country and India in their long-standing conflict over Kashmir.

"The United States is the only superpower in the world today, it has a lot of influence, and I do believe third-party mediation is necessary to resolve the Kashmir dispute," she said on CNN's "Evans & Novak" programme.

Two days ago at the United Nations, Bhutto proposed convening an ambitious international conference to deal with Kashmir, international arms control and "the danger of a nuclear arms race in South Asia."

"I believe the Clinton administration is hesitant in mediating unless mediation is acceptable to both parties," Bhutto told CNN, "but I hope that in the wake of the Indian refusal to sign (the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty), post-election the American administration will review the South Asian situation and perhaps see why Pakistan has always argued that mediation is necessary."

India has blocked the formal activation of the test-ban treaty because it does not contain a timetable for the destruction of existing nuclear arsenals. Both Moslem-majority Pakistan and its neighbour, mainly Hindu India, are believed to have nuclear weapons or the ability to assemble them quickly.
Since a separatist revolt erupted in 1990 in Jammu and Kashmir, India's only Moslem-majority state, more than 20,000 people have been killed, according to police and hospital officials.

Thousands of joyful Kashmiris turned out on Saturday to greet their new leader, Farooq Abdullah, when he arrived in Srinagar, the summer capital, after a landslide victory in the first local elections since 1990.

Abdullah's moderate National Conference won on a promise of greater autonomy for the Himalayan state, but dozens of Kashmiri separatist groups fighting for freedom or closer ties to Pakistan have already rejected his government.

Asked about another of Pakistan's neighbours, Afghanistan, Bhutto said Pakistan had not assisted the Taleban, the fundamentalist Islamic movement that captured the capital, Kabul, late last month. She expressed hope that the movement would end factionalism and bloodshed "and not interfere northwards or southwards."
On heightened Israeli-Palestinian tensions, she said Pakistan had been "deeply disturbed by recent trends which show that (the Middle East) peace process may be jeopardised."
